topics.title: Carotid Anatomy & Normal Values
topics.quickSummary: The ICA supplies the brain (low resistance), while the ECA supplies the face/scalp (high resistance). Understanding these differences is critical for exam success.
clinicalPearls: Carotid exam performed with patient supine, neck slightly extended, head turned away from side being scanned
ICA = Internal Carotid Artery (low resistance vessel)
ECA = External Carotid Artery (high resistance vessel)
Vertebral arteries evaluated as part of cerebrovascular assessment
70-99% carotid stenosis is a CRITICAL FINDING requiring immediate attention
Linear array transducer used for carotid exams

sections.title: ICA vs ECA Characteristics
sections.content:
ICA (Internal Carotid Artery): Low resistance vessel supplying brain. Continuous forward diastolic flow throughout cardiac cycle. Longer acceleration time. PI < 1.0 is normal.

ECA (External Carotid Artery): High resistance vessel supplying face/scalp. Minimal or reversed diastolic flow. Similar pattern to resting extremity arteries.

sections.title: Normal Values
sections.content:
ICA has increased acceleration time (AT) compared to high resistance vessels due to low resistance
AT longer in ICA and cerebral vessels vs extremity arteries
Brain vessels: Pulsatility Index (PI) normally <1.0
ICA waveform: low resistance with continuous forward diastolic flow
ECA waveform: high resistance with minimal/reversed diastolic flow

keyTakeaways: ICA = low resistance (brain needs constant perfusion)
AT longer in ICA than extremities

topics.title: Doppler Principles & Angle
topics.quickSummary: Doppler angle must be <60°. At 90°: no shift detected. At 0°: maximum shift. Frequency shift proportional to velocity and cos(angle).
clinicalPearls: Doppler effect: frequency shift when sound reflects from moving object
Flow toward transducer = positive frequency shift (above baseline)
Flow away from transducer = negative frequency shift (below baseline)
Frequency shift proportional to blood velocity

sections.title: Basic Doppler Principles
sections.content:
Doppler effect: frequency shift when sound reflects from moving object
Flow toward transducer = positive frequency shift (above baseline)
Flow away from transducer = negative frequency shift (below baseline)
Frequency shift proportional to blood velocity
Angle dependency critical for accuracy

Doppler Equation: Frequency shift = (2 × velocity × transmitted frequency × cos angle) / speed of sound

sections.title: Angle Correction
sections.content:
Doppler angle should be <60 degrees (ideally 45-60°)
At 90°: cos(90°) = 0, no Doppler shift detected
At 0°: cos(0°) = 1, maximum Doppler shift
Larger angles = greater error in velocity calculation
Angle correction cursor must be parallel to vessel wall/blood flow

Angle correction line must align with flow direction

Distal occlusion causes increased resistance proximally = high RI

Measures variability in blood velocity during cardiac cycle
Distinguishes inflow from outflow disease
Not dependent on angle

sections.title: Bernoulli Effect

Total fluid energy remains constant
Pressure energy + kinetic energy = constant
Velocity increase = pressure decrease
Velocity decrease = pressure increase

Fast blood (at stenosis) = less pressure on vessel walls
Reduced pressure at stenosis with increased velocity
After stenosis: velocity decreases, pressure increases
Explains pressure drop across stenosis

Occurs in systole in large vessels

topics.title: Critical Velocity Criteria
topics.quickSummary: Master the key PSV thresholds for diagnosing stenosis across all vascular territories - these are high-yield exam questions!
clinicalPearls: Celiac artery >70% stenosis: PSV > 225 cm/s (most tested abdominal vessel)
Renal artery stenosis indicators: Tardus parvus waveform, AT >70ms, AI <3 m/s
Peripheral artery stenosis: PSV ratio >2.0, PSV >200 cm/s
Hemodialysis access stenosis: PSV >400 cm/s or PSV ratio >2:1
Post-meal response: SMA velocity doubles, minimal celiac change
Renal arteries have the LOWEST resistive index among abdominal vessels

sections.title: Abdominal Velocity Criteria
sections.content:
Celiac Artery >70% Stenosis: PSV > 225 cm/s
Renal Artery Stenosis: Tardus parvus in segmental arteries, Acceleration time > 70 ms, Acceleration index < 3 m/s
SMA Post-Meal Response: Velocity doubles (normal response to feeding)
Celiac Post-Meal: Minimal velocity change

sections.title: Peripheral Artery Stenosis
sections.content:
Significant Stenosis: PSV ratio >2.0, PSV >200 cm/s
Prolonged AT: >200 ms suggests proximal stenosis
Location: Use segmental approach to identify level

sections.title: Hemodialysis Access
sections.content:
Stenosis Criteria: PSV >400 cm/s OR PSV ratio >2:1
Maturation Time: 1-3 months typical for AVF
Ideal Flow: >600 mL/min for adequate dialysis
Vein Requirements: >6mm diameter, <6mm depth from skin

topics.title: Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) & Pressure Measurements
topics.quickSummary: ABI is the cornerstone of PAD diagnosis. Know the interpretation ranges and what to do when values are abnormal.
clinicalPearls: ABI >1.30-1.40 suggests medial calcification (non-compressible vessels) - measure TOE pressures instead
ABI <0.90 = PAD, <0.50 = SEVERE PAD requiring urgent evaluation
Exercise ABI decrease >20% suggests PAD even if resting ABI is normal
First symptom of PAD: Intermittent claudication
Toe pressure normal: >30 mmHg (use when vessels non-compressible)
Segmental pressure gradient >30 mmHg indicates stenosis at that level

sections.title: ABI Interpretation
sections.content:
Normal: 0.90 - 1.30 (routine follow-up)
PAD: < 0.90 (further evaluation needed)
Severe PAD: < 0.50 (urgent vascular evaluation)
Calcified Vessels: > 1.30-1.40 (falsely elevated - measure toe pressures)

Exercise ABI: Decrease >20% from baseline suggests PAD
Clinical Pearl: Some patients with normal resting ABI have PAD revealed only with exercise testing

sections.title: When ABI Fails
sections.content:
Medial Calcification Problem: Diabetes, renal disease, elderly patients may have non-compressible vessels
Falsely Elevated ABI: >1.30-1.40 suggests calcification
Solution: Measure TOE PRESSURES instead
Normal Toe Pressure: >30 mmHg
Toe-Brachial Index: Can be calculated when ABI unreliable

sections.title: Segmental Pressures & PVR
sections.content:
Normal Gradient: <20-30 mmHg between consecutive levels
Significant Drop: >30 mmHg suggests stenosis at that level
Levels Tested: High thigh, low thigh, calf, ankle, toe

PVR Waveforms:
Normal: Sharp systolic upstroke, dicrotic notch
Mild Disease: Loss of dicrotic notch
Moderate/Severe: Flattened, delayed waveform

topics.title: Venous System Diagnostic Criteria
topics.quickSummary: DVT diagnosis relies on non-compressibility. Reflux diagnosis requires >0.5 seconds of reversed flow. Master these criteria!
clinicalPearls: PRIMARY DVT criterion: Non-compressibility of vein (gold standard)
Augmentation failure suggests PROXIMAL obstruction (not at compression site)
Thigh tourniquet normalization = GSV reflux; Calf tourniquet = perforator reflux
Loss of phasicity may indicate proximal obstruction OR chronic changes

sections.title: DVT Evaluation
sections.content:
Primary Diagnostic Criterion: NON-COMPRESSIBILITY of vein
Compression Technique: Gentle but firm pressure with transducer
Positive Finding: Vein walls do not coapt completely

Secondary Signs:
- Loss of phasicity (suggests proximal obstruction)
- Augmentation failure (proximal obstruction)
- Visible thrombus
- Venous dilation
- Absent or dampened flow

sections.title: Venous Reflux Testing
sections.content:
Reflux Duration Criteria: >0.5 seconds indicates valve incompetence
Testing Method: Augmentation with distal compression + release OR Valsalva
Normal Response: Brief reversal (<0.5 sec) then competent valves close
Abnormal: Prolonged retrograde flow >0.5 seconds

Venous Refill Time (VRT):
Normal: >20 seconds
Abnormal: <20 seconds (suggests reflux/incompetence)
Testing: Patient stands, empties veins, observe refill time

sections.title: Tourniquet Testing for Reflux Source
sections.content:
Purpose: Identify SOURCE of venous reflux

Thigh Tourniquet Application:
VRT normalizes → Great Saphenous Vein (GSV) reflux
Reflux eliminated with superficial system compression

Calf Tourniquet Application:
VRT normalizes → Perforator vein reflux
Incompetent perforators allowing deep-to-superficial flow

No Normalization:
Deep venous insufficiency
May require surgical intervention

topics.title: Key Pathology & Clinical Associations
topics.quickSummary: Know the classic disease presentations and demographic associations - these appear frequently on exams!
clinicalPearls: Blue toe syndrome = microemboli from PROXIMAL source (aortoiliac disease, aneurysm, ulcerated plaque)
Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD): Young women, MID-TO-DISTAL renal artery, 'string of beads'
Buerger's disease: Young MALE smokers, small/medium vessels, distal (tibial/digital)
Popliteal artery = MOST COMMON peripheral aneurysm location
Leriche syndrome triad: Claudication + impotence + diminished femoral pulses
Paget-von-Schroetter: Effort-induced subclavian/axillary DVT in young athletes

sections.title: Classic Disease Demographics
sections.content:
Fibromuscular Dysplasia (FMD):
Demographics: Young to middle-aged WOMEN
Vessels: Renal arteries (most common), carotid
Location: MID-TO-DISTAL renal artery (vs atherosclerosis = proximal/ostial)
Appearance: 'String of beads' appearance

Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans):
Demographics: Young MALE smokers (<45 years)
Vessels: Small and medium arteries
Location: DISTAL vessels (tibial, digital)
Pattern: Segmental involvement

Paget-von-Schroetter Disease:
Demographics: Young adults, athletes
Presentation: Effort-induced subclavian/axillary vein thrombosis
Risk Factors: Repetitive arm motion, thoracic outlet syndrome

sections.title: Pathognomonic Findings
sections.content:
Blue Toe Syndrome:
Cause: Microemboli from proximal source
Associations: Aortoiliac occlusive disease, AAA, ulcerated plaque
Presentation: Ischemic toes with palpable pulses (embolic, not flow-limiting)

Leriche Syndrome:
Definition: Aortoiliac occlusive disease
Classic Triad:
1. Buttock/thigh claudication
2. Impotence (males)
3. Diminished/absent femoral pulses

Subclavian Steal:
Finding: REVERSED flow in vertebral artery
Cause: Proximal subclavian stenosis/occlusion
Symptoms: Arm claudication + vertebrobasilar insufficiency

sections.title: Aneurysm Essentials
sections.content:
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):
Definition: >3 cm diameter (or >1.5x normal)
Surveillance:
- 3.0-3.9 cm: Annually
- 4.0-4.9 cm: Every 6 months
- ≥5.0 cm: Consider repair, close monitoring

Peripheral Aneurysms:
Most Common Location: POPLITEAL artery
Complications: Thrombosis, embolization, rupture (less common than AAA)
Association: 50% bilateral, often associated with AAA

keyTakeaways: FMD = young women, mid-distal renal artery
Buerger's = young male smokers, distal vessels
Blue toe = microemboli from proximal source

topics.title: Follow-Up Intervals & Surveillance
topics.quickSummary: Know when to bring patients back after procedures and for aneurysm surveillance - critical for clinical practice!
clinicalPearls: Post-carotid endarterectomy (CEA): 1-3 months first follow-up to detect restenosis
AAA 4.0-4.9 cm: Every 6 months surveillance (increased rupture risk)
Renal artery post-intervention: 1, 6, 12 months, then annually
Post-intervention surveillance critical for detecting restenosis
AAA ≥5.0 cm: Consider repair, very close monitoring if not surgical candidate

sections.title: Post-Surgical Follow-Up
sections.content:
Post-Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA):
First Follow-Up: 1-3 months
Purpose: Detect restenosis at surgical site
Subsequent: 6 months, 12 months, then annually
Findings: Assess patency, look for intimal hyperplasia

Renal Artery Stent/Angioplasty:
Protocol: 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, then annually
Criteria: PSV, RAR (renal-aortic ratio)
Restenosis Risk: Highest in first 6-12 months

Hemodialysis Access:
New Access: Weekly until mature (1-3 months)
Mature Access: Every 3-4 months for surveillance
Problem Access: As needed for stenosis/thrombosis evaluation

sections.title: AAA Surveillance
sections.content:
3.0-3.9 cm Diameter:
Interval: ANNUALLY
Rupture Risk: Low (<1% per year)
Action: Continue surveillance

4.0-4.9 cm Diameter:
Interval: Every 6 MONTHS
Rupture Risk: Moderate (1-11% per year depending on size)
Action: Close monitoring, discuss surgical options

≥5.0 cm Diameter:
Interval: Very close monitoring (3 months or less)
Rupture Risk: High (>10% per year for 5.5+ cm)
Action: Strong consideration for surgical repair

Rapid Expansion:
>0.5 cm in 6 months: Refer for surgical evaluation regardless of size

keyTakeaways: Rapid AAA expansion >0.5 cm/6 mo = urgent
